summary: Presents SLAPP, one proposal for a protocol between wireless termination points and access controllers, aiming at interoperability between vendors for the CAPWAP problem. This is a historic document.

eli5.summary: Different brands of wifi boxes and boss computers need a shared language. This memo is one idea for that language, proposed during the search for a standard.

subtitle: A protocol for controllers to discover and manage wireless access points from different vendors.

tldr.problem: Wireless networks need a way for controllers at one vendor to manage wireless access points from other vendors, but different vendors use incompatible solutions. The CAPWAP problem asks for interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: SLAPP divides the solution into a technology-independent framework and pluggable technology-specific control protocols. Devices discover each other, establish DTLS security, then negotiate which control protocol to use.
tldr.outcome: SLAPP was a historical proposal in the search for a standard wireless access point control protocol. It was later superseded by RFC 5415, which became the CAPWAP standard.

today: RFC 5413 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 5415, which became the IETF standards-track solution for CAPWAP. SLAPP should not be used as the basis for any Internet deployment.

sections.title: The CAPWAP Problem
sections.content:
Large wireless networks need a way for a central controller to manage many wireless access points (called Wireless Termination Points or WTPs). The challenge is that these devices come from different vendors, and vendors historically used incompatible control protocols. The Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP) problem asks: how can a controller from Vendor A control access points from Vendor B?

SLAPP (Secure Light Access Point Protocol) proposes a solution by splitting the problem into two layers. A common framework handles discovery, security, and negotiation in a vendor-neutral way. On top of that, pluggable control protocols handle the details specific to 802.11 networks or other technologies.
sections.eli5: Instead of each company inventing its own language, SLAPP provides a common way for them to introduce themselves and agree on how to talk. Then they can choose different languages for the actual work.

sections.title: Framework and Topologies
sections.content:
SLAPP supports multiple network topologies. A WTP and its controller can be directly connected, on the same local network, separated by routers, or even across the public Internet. The protocol is designed to work across all these cases.

SLAPP defines a clear separation between the device types: WTPs (the access point hardware) and ACs (the central management controller). The protocol also distinguishes between two common wireless architectures. In Local MAC mode, the WTP handles all 802.11 frame processing. In Split MAC mode, some functions are split between the WTP and AC, such as encryption or authentication.
sections.eli5: SLAPP works whether the control box is in the same closet, the same building, or across the country. It also knows about two main ways to organize wifi hardware: where one box does everything, or where the controller and access point share the jobs.

sections.title: Discovery and Security Handshake
sections.content:
When a WTP powers up, it needs to find a suitable controller. SLAPP defines a discovery process that tries multiple methods: static configuration, DHCP options, DNS queries, broadcast, and IP multicast. The WTP sends a Discover Request packet listing its hardware version, software version, and the control protocols it supports.

A controller that receives the request and wants to manage the WTP sends a Discover Response. Once discovered, the AC initiates a DTLS (Datagram Transport Layer Security) handshake with the WTP to establish an encrypted and authenticated channel. DTLS is chosen because it provides security over UDP and includes fragmentation and reassembly. After the DTLS handshake succeeds, they enter the negotiated control protocol phase.
sections.eli5: The access point shouts out 'Is anyone there?' using several methods until someone answers. Once found, they do a secret handshake (DTLS) to make sure they trust each other before they start working together.

sections.title: SLAPP Message Format
sections.content:
All SLAPP messages begin with a 4-byte header. The first 4 bits indicate the major version, the next 4 bits the minor version (currently 1.0). The next 8 bits specify the message type: discover request, discover response, control protocol packet, or image download control. The final 2 bytes give the total message length in bytes.

Version negotiation is important: if peers support different major versions, the older major version is used. Minor version differences do not prevent communication; the peer simply omits features of the newer minor version. Messages are retransmitted by the initiator if no response arrives within a configurable timeout, with up to five total attempts.
sections.eli5: Every message starts with a small label saying what version it is and what kind of message it is. If one side is newer, they talk in the older way both understand.

sections.title: Negotiated Control Protocols
sections.content:
SLAPP itself is just the framework. On top of it, specific control protocols are negotiated and used. The RFC defines two example protocols. The first is an 802.11-specific protocol that handles wireless configuration: setting channel, power, encryption, ESSID, and managing virtual access points. Information is exchanged using Information Elements (IEs), each with a type, length, and value. The second is a generic Image Download Protocol that allows the controller to push firmware updates to WTPs.

The 802.11 control protocol defines message types for registration, configuration, status queries, statistics, key management, and keepalives. Each message type carries specific IEs appropriate to its purpose, allowing controllers to push configuration updates and WTPs to report their current state and capabilities.
sections.eli5: After the handshake, they agree to use a specific control protocol. For wifi, one protocol handles things like channels and passwords. Another generic protocol is for updating the access point's firmware.

sections.title: Historic Status and Replacement
sections.content:
SLAPP was submitted to the IETF as a basis for further work in the CAPWAP Working Group. It was published as Historic in February 2010. RFC 5415, published at the same time, documents the IETF standards-track CAPWAP solution, which obsoletes SLAPP and any mechanisms defined in this RFC.

The IESG note states that SLAPP was not thoroughly reviewed and may contain errors. It should not be used as a basis for deployment. RFC 5415 is the standard to use for any implementation of wireless access point control protocols.
sections.eli5: This protocol was a proposal during the search for a standard. The actual standard that won is RFC 5415. This RFC is kept as a historical record of the competing ideas.
